zones.name: Animals in Nature and Mythology
zones.intro_short:
In this zone we discover some of the incredible animal species that call Southeast Asia home.
Historically, Southeast Asian societies understood the places of animals within ecological systems. This familiarity came about as a result of generations of close observations of animal morphology, anatomy and traits and led to communities incorporating elements of the natural world into their spiritual and social lives.
zones.body_full:
In this zone we discover some of the incredible animal species that call Southeast Asia home.
Historically, Southeast Asian societies understood the places of animals within ecological systems. This familiarity came about as a result of generations of close observations of animal morphology, anatomy and traits and led to communities incorporating elements of the natural world into their spiritual and social lives. For example, the iridescent spiral of a seashell made it valuable as an ornament, a ritual object and a currency. At the same time, the chicken became part of local culinary traditions, while the rooster's signature alertness was frequently invoked in domestic design.
With the weaving of elements of the natural world into the region’s rich spiritual tapestry, the forms of real animals such as crocodiles, birds, snakes, elephants and fish inspired mythical creatures such as the dragon, phoenix, naga, makara and the Garuda

zones.intro_short: The second zone allows you to explore the presence of animals across science, technology, religion, cosmology, myth and lore. Together, these bodies of knowledge and belief constitute Southeast Asia’s vibrant intangible cultural heritage.
zones.body_full:
The second zone allows you to explore the presence of animals across science, technology, religion, cosmology, myth and lore. Together, these bodies of knowledge and belief constitute Southeast Asia’s vibrant intangible cultural heritage.
Across the region, animals provide communities with a language for understanding and navigating the unseen worlds. Through the animal kingdom, people have expressed complex ideas about creation, morality, power, protection and the human relationship to the cosmos. In the case of  traditional cosmological systems, which often conceive the universe as tripartite, animals were used to symbolize each level: the upper world of the heavens is inhabited by spirits, so is symbolized by birds; the middle world, the earthly domain, rests securely upon the back of a vast creature like a turtle; and the underworld is associated with subterranean or deep-water-dwelling animals. Based on this understanding, ancestral spirits and divine messengers are believed to manifest as birds such as the hornbill, while the role of bridging different cosmological spheres is fulfilled by mythical creatures such as the phoenix, which combine the traits of multiple animals.
Animals also serve as a lens for thinking about human society. In regional folklore, they act as allegorical stand-ins for our own virtues and vices – such as the trickster mouse-deer outwitting the crocodile to teach a lesson of the importance of wit regardless of size. In daily life, the rooster’s crow marks the rhythms of time and symbolizes diligence. The qualities associated with animals are also represented in the materials, forms and motifs used by artisans to create items for household and ritual use.
As you explore these displays, you will see that animals do not just inhabit our environments; they symbolize how the cosmos operates. They are an essential creative repertoire through which the peoples of Southeast Asia express their spirituality and deep connection to their communities.

zones.intro_short: The third zone of the exhibition explores the presence of animals and mythological creatures in art, rituals, festivals and everyday life. zones.body_full:
The third zone of the exhibition explores the presence of animals and mythological creatures in art, rituals, festivals and everyday life. This zone displays carefully crafted objects valued for their practical functions, spiritual meanings and aesthetic beauty. Whether featuring in daily life, rituals or decoratively, such objects have long been part of Southeast Asia’s rich tangible cultural heritage, shaping life across the region.
The diverse items on display include tools, weapons and vessels. For example, in southern Thai culture, cylinders made of bamboo, wood and animal horn (fire pistons) were used in pre-modern times as tools for kindling fires and doubled as protective talismans capable of warding off danger. Across Malay and Javanese cultures, a traditional weapon – the keris – when inscribed with auspicious bird motifs such as the kingfisher and the Garuda, gained spiritual power. Likewise, sireh (betel nut) sets and ceramic wares adorned with motifs of fish, cranes and phoenixes gained the attributes associated with these auspicious animals to invoke wealth, longevity, stability and prestige. These items reveal how incorporating the traits of such animals into an object’s design activated their inherent energies.

zones.name: The Curious Minds’ Play Zone
name_variants: The Curious Minds’ Play Zone (style sheet node 670:1118)
zones.intro_short:
This zone invites you to carry the journey beyond the screen. Visiting one of our ten partner museums across five countries? Pick up a Shared Heritage Passport, scan the QR codes beside featured objects to follow the animal trails, and collect a sticker for each one you complete. Then play Maker of Myth to sketch a brand-new artefact and leave a message of peace.
For teachers and museum educators, explore ready-to-use education materials for Along Animal Trails: Creations that Bind Southeast Asia, and download Understanding Shared Histories, a UNESCO teaching package for lower secondary classrooms.
